question: How did David kill Goliath?
summary: 1 Samuel 17:49-50 says David killed Goliath with a sling and a stone and that "there was no sword in the hand of David." The very next verse, 1 Samuel 17:51, has David running over, drawing Goliath's own sword, and killing him with it. Within two verses Goliath dies twice by two different weapons.

reconcile.connective: Harmonizers read the two verses as one continuous act: the stone felled and stunned Goliath, and David finished him with the giant's own sword.

discrepancy.connective: The objection is catalogued by skeptic-compiler Donald Morgan, who lists the two verses side by side and asks whether David killed Goliath twice — once with the slingstone and again with the sword.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on 1 Samuel 17:51
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this exact passage, explaining that the stone only stunned Goliath and that David then dispatched him with the giant's own sword — the harmonizing reading keyed to 1 Samuel 17:50-51. Used as the PD anchor because Haley's coverage of this specific verse pair could not be confirmed.

excerpts.excerpt_text: for it seems that by the blow of the stone he was only stunned, and fell to the ground, but still had life in him, which David soon put an end to by his own sword …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly reconciles 17:50 (no sword) with 17:51 (sword): the stone only stunned Goliath, who was then finished with the sword — the single strongest harmonization, parity-capped to match the lone named-skeptic on a discrepancy_first row.
excerpts.source_note_text:
Therefore David ran and stood upon the Philistine,.... Upon his carcass, as it lay prostrate on the ground, and trampled on him, in just contempt of him who had defied, reproached, and despised the armies of Israel:
and took his sword, and drew it out of the sheath thereof; which no doubt was a very large one, and required a good deal of strength to unsheathe it, and use it; and therefore either David, though so very young, was naturally very strong, or he had at this time a more than ordinary measure of strength given him:
and slew him; for it seems that by the blow of the stone he was only stunned, and fell to the ground, but still had life in him, which David soon put an end to by his own sword:
and cut off his head therewith; by which it would appear to both armies looking on that his business was done, and he was thoroughly dispatched:
and when the Philistines saw their champion was dead; of which the cutting off his head was a demonstrative proof, and which they could discern at a distance:
they fled; being struck with a panic at this unexpected event, and no doubt by the Lord; for otherwise, had they given themselves the least time to reflect on their own numbers and strength, they had no just occasion to flee; their safety not depending on a single man, though ever so strong: upon this occasion David penned the ninth psalm; see Psa 9:1.
